newsitem.title: UK: Cobalt underpinned by Zaire, antimony marks time.
newsitem.headline: Cobalt underpinned by Zaire, antimony marks time.

text.p: Fighting in Zaire helped to firm cobalt prices on minor metals markets this week, but high grade prices looked to be finding resistance above $25 a pound, traders said.

Elsewhere the bulls and bears of the antimony market continued to debate over the markets true direction, while indium moved to build a base above $300 a kilo after the recent rally against a backdrop of short supply.
Concerns about supply from Zaire following the fall of Lubumbashi to rebel forces helped to buoy cobalt.
"There has been some consumer covering on Zaire, though they do not seem to be building up their stocks...most are buying enough metal for a month's supply," one trader said.

Industry officials believe output in the mineral-rich Shaba region may be briefly disrupted but that fighting will soon end and any new government may invest more money in Zaire's ailing minerals industry.
State metals producer Gecamines closed its headquarters in Lubumbashi on Monday as rebels advanced.
Traders said anyone who secured effective control of Shaba region would not want to curtail production of a hard currency earner such as cobalt.

Zaire has recently been producing around 5,000 tonnes of cobalt and 40,000 tonnes of copper a year. The copper is marginal to world supply but the cobalt represents about a fifth of global supply of all grades of the metal.
Analysts say stocks of up to 600 tonnes are adequate for the time being.

Cobalt traders also focused on the U.S. Stockpile sale, which was still on hold. The sale of U.S. government stockpiled cobalt will remain on hold until further notice as legal processes continue, a U.S. official said.
The Stockpile was asked last week by a Federal Claims Court judge for additional information about its sales policy.

Minor Metals, a trading company, sought a restraining order on the March 31 sealed bid sale for one million pounds of cobalt because it was unhappy with the lack of an "all or none" clause in the sales contracts.
The Stockpile wants the freedom to award just some of the metal requested by any bidder. The March 31 sale was postponed until April 7 and then cancelled until further notice.
Lower graded Russian material was trading around $22 a pound.
Traders said two shipments of Russian metal were to be delivered into Rotterdam warehouses this week. The rumoured 300-tonne shipments were helping to dampen upside sentiment.
No clear picture was emerging in the opaque antimony market as market operators remained divided about the market's next move.
Several suggested prices had the potential to rally above $2,500 resistance towards $2,800/$3,000, while others said prices were generally set to firm but a downside correction was looming.
"It has gone up but is losing upside momentum and is due for a fall," one trader commented.
The trader said the higher numbers mentioned were largely due to market manoeuvring by operators holding long positions.
The fundamental picture was helping to support the view for higher prices.

A recent meeting of Chinese smelters and miners decided to limit production to boost the market. That and transport problems created by the rainy season in Bolivia were cited as two factors behind higher prices.
There was also talk that Chinese custom and trade officials were attempting to stamp out smuggling in many of China's ports.

Indium at one stage traded as high as $340 a kilo before drifting back to settle just above $300. Traders said indium, against the backdrop of low stocks and brisk Japanese consumer demand, could reach $400 a kilo in the near term.
Major producer China was still not selling into the market, while the handful of Western producers were said to be sold out.
Indium Corp of America in raised its list prices to $335 a kilo from $315.
